https://www.dw.com/en/germany-condemns-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J6bT Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has triggered outrage in Germany Image: EyalWarshavsky/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO Advertisement "I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza," said Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, on Monday , sparking worldwide outrage. The hard-liner in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's Cabinet also described exactly what he had in mind: Every night, 30 or 40 Palestinians should be "removed." Ben-Gvir emphasized that he was not only referring to militant Palestinians who posed an immediate threat, adding that there are people in the Gaza Strip who do not deserve to live. On Wednesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz denounced the statement made by the controversial Israeli politician. "The chancellor strongly condemns Minister Ben-Gvir's inhumane statements, which violate international law — they are unacceptable," said a government spokesperson in Berlin. Merz is officially on vacation. Ben-Gvir Gaza comments trigger condemnation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The spokesperson also criticized Israel's plans to further accelerate settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank . Merz is following the latest developments "with great concern." The spokesperson said there must be no further steps toward annexation, adding: "As the occupying power, Israel must treat Palestinians with dignity, protect their property and ensure public administration and humanitarian aid." Vice Chancellor Klingbeil: 'A line has truly been crossed' Merz's deputy from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil , had already called for consequences on Tuesday. "These are statements that we, as the federal government, cannot accept in any way," he told the private TV station Sat1. Klingbeil said that sanctions are being discussed at the European level, adding: "This must now be looked at very seriously." Despite all its solidarity with the state of Israel, Germany must not remain silent, he stressed. A line has now "truly been crossed." Hildegard Bentele, a German member of the European Parliament from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also supports sanctions against Ben-Gvir, telling DW on Tuesday that she had been calling for them for a year. "Eliminating individuals is unacceptable to us in Europe," she emphasized. Many countries have imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir Several countries have already imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir, including Australia, France , the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Norway and the Netherlands. Jürgen Hardt, the foreign policy spokesperson for the conservative parliamentary group in Germany's lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, also supports the call for European Union sanctions against Ben-Gvir. "The EU should sanction him as a statement on the universal validity of human dignity and human rights ," Hardt told the news magazine Politico . Hardt said he is convinced that an Israeli Cabinet without Ben-Gvir would bring Europe and Israel closer together again. Calls for sanctions and a halt to arms exports to Israel The environmentalist Green Party , an opposition party in the German parliament, has also demanded harsh consequences. "I urge the federal government to impose an entry ban on this man and to advocate for similar sanctions to be imposed at the European level as well," Green Party leader Franziska Brantner told Politico . How Germany's Left Party is split over anti-Zionism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This is not the first time Ben-Gvir has drawn attention for his appalling calls for violence against Palestinians, Brantner emphasized. She also called for Germany to follow the example of other countries and impose sanctions: "It's time for Germany to join these nations." Lea Reisner, a politician from the socialist Left Party , went further on Deutschlandfunk public radio, calling for a halt to all German arms exports to Israel . Josef Schuster: Ben-Gvir's comments 'deeply shameful and irresponsible' Germany's Central Council of Jews in Germany also reacted with horror to Ben-Gvir's call for mass killings of Palestinians. The president of the Central Council, Josef Schuster, told the Catholic News Agency that Ben-Gvir's statements were diametrically opposed to Jewish values and damage Israel's reputation. "Itamar Ben-Gvir's behavior is deeply shameful and irresponsible," said Schuster, adding that it illustrates the danger posed by far-right forces. Kirsten Fehrs, chair of the Council of the Protestant Church in Germany, described Ben-Gvir's statements on the social media platform Threads as an "attack on humanity." The bishop stressed that there must be a shared conviction across religions that every human being possesses inalienable dignity because they are made in God's image. "No one can bestow this dignity, and no one can take it away," she said. This article was originally written in German. Illustration: Storm-1679/Microsoft Threat Analysis Center Disinfo black ops Cyberwar Analysis How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation stokes division and sows despair Dan Milmo and Robert Booth Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.38 EDT Share Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies. The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise slamming the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation. Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago. New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UN Read more The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots. It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence . “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said. Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”. Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats. “You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says. Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”. Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks” this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning. It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption. The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says. It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals . Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards Read more One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic. The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect. Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”. Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service. Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”. The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns. One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News. Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024. The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | Editorial Read more Robert Topinka , reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them. He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather he said Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it. “What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka. AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns. The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models. The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.
